name: Takht Sri Keshgarh Sahib
deity: Guru Granth Sahib (Takht of the Khalsa)
significance: One of the five Takhts, the supreme seats of Sikh temporal authority, standing where Guru Gobind Singh inaugurated the Khalsa in 1699. The shrine occupies the site of Anandgarh Qila, one of the forts the Guru raised at Anandpur, and the present building dates from a reconstruction in the mid-1930s.

name: Takht Sri Damdama Sahib
significance: The fifth Sikh Takht, founded in 1705 where Guru Gobind Singh rested after the Anandpur campaigns and dictated the definitive recension of the Guru Granth Sahib to Bhai Mani Singh. The scholarly work done here earned the place the title 'Guru Ki Kashi'; it was recognised as a Takht by the SGPC in 1966 and confirmed by the Indian government in 1999.

name: Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib
significance: A Takht of Sikhism raised over the spot where Guru Gobind Singh held his last court and was cremated in 1708, the inner chamber being called Angitha Sahib. The present building was constructed between 1832 and 1837 under Maharaja Ranjit Singh; it was here that the Guru declared the Guru Granth Sahib his successor.

name: Gurdwara Bangla Sahib
deity: Guru Granth Sahib (associated with Guru Har Krishan)
significance: Delhi's largest gurdwara, built around the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh where the eighth Guru, Har Krishan, stayed in 1664 and tended the city's sick. Sardar Baghel Singh converted the site into a shrine in 1783 as one of nine Sikh shrines he raised in Delhi, and most of the present structure dates from after 1947; its sarovar measures about 225 by 235 feet.
story: Devotees hold that the water of the temple's sarovar, sanctified during Guru Har Krishan's stay, carries healing power.

name: Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib
deity: Guru Granth Sahib (martyrdom site of Guru Tegh Bahadur)
significance: Marks the place in Chandni Chowk where the ninth Guru, Tegh Bahadur, was beheaded on Aurangzeb's orders on 11 November 1675. Baghel Singh of the Karora Misl negotiated with Shah Alam II to build the first shrine here in 1783; after litigation under British rule was settled in the Sikhs' favour, the present building was raised in 1930 by Rai Bahadur Narain Singh.

name: Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib
deity: Guru Granth Sahib (memorial to the younger Sahibzade)
builtDisplay: built 1843; upper storeys and domes added 1955
significance: Commemorates the execution of Guru Gobind Singh's two youngest sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, who were bricked up alive in December 1705 after refusing to convert. The gurdwara was built in 1843 on a square plan with a ribbed lotus dome and cusped arches, and its upper levels were added in 1955; its basement holds a Guru Granth Sahib copy and relics linked to the events.

name: Gurdwara Sri Darbar Sahib, Tarn Taran
significance: The principal Sikh shrine of Tarn Taran, founded by the fifth Guru, Arjan Dev, and set beside a large sarovar in the centre of the town. Guru Arjan also established a leper asylum here, which passed to Christian missionaries in 1858; control of the gurdwara transferred to the SGPC on 27 January 1921 during the Gurdwara Reform Movement.

name: Gurdwara Baoli Sahib, Goindwal
deity: Guru Granth Sahib (Baoli Sahib of Guru Amar Das)
significance: Built around the eighty-four-step stepwell that Guru Amar Das sank in 1551, after which he moved the Sikh centre from Khadur to Goindwal on becoming Guru. The shrine carries a large fluted dome with a gold pinnacle, four cupolas and frescoes illustrating the Guru's life, and pilgrims recite the Japji Sahib at each of the baoli's steps.
story: Tradition tells of a trader named Goinda who could not found a settlement here because of local superstition, until Amar Das, through his service and devotion, cleared the obstacle and the village was established.

name: Gurdwara Ber Sahib, Sultanpur Lodhi
deity: Guru Granth Sahib (associated with Guru Nanak)
significance: Stands on the bank of the Kali Bein at Sultanpur Lodhi, the site Sikh tradition identifies with the revelation that began Guru Nanak's mission. The present building was begun in 1937–38 and completed in 1941–42 under Maharaja Jagatjit Singh of Kapurthala, and takes its name from a ber (jujube) tree said to have been planted by the Guru.
story: The janamsakhis relate that in 1499 Guru Nanak entered the Kali Bein to bathe, vanished for three days, and emerged declaring 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.'

name: Gurudwara Nanak Jhira Sahib
deity: Guru Granth Sahib (associated with Guru Nanak)
significance: Marks Guru Nanak's visit to Bidar during his second southern missionary journey (1510–1514) and the perennial spring, the Nanak Jhira, that has flowed at the spot ever since. The gurdwara was built in 1948 and draws four to five lakh pilgrims a year, with a continuous langar and a museum honouring Guru Tegh Bahadur.
story: It is said that, moved by the villagers' shortage of water, Guru Nanak moved a stone aside with his wooden sandal and a stream of cool fresh water sprang out.

name: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib Kartarpur
deity: Guru Granth Sahib (site of Guru Nanak's last years)
significance: One of Sikhism's holiest sites, on the Ravi where Guru Nanak founded the town of Kartarpur in 1504 and spent his last eighteen years running a langar and a working farming community until his death in 1539. The main shrine was built in 1925 at a cost of Rs 1,35,600 funded by the Maharaja of Patiala, and the complex was enlarged in 2004 and again in 2018 for the Kartarpur Corridor.
story: When Hindus and Muslims quarrelled over the Guru's body, it is said the shawl covering him was lifted to reveal only flowers, which the two communities divided between them to cremate and to bury.

name: Gurdwara Janam Asthan
deity: Guru Granth Sahib (birthplace of Guru Nanak)
significance: Built over the house where Guru Nanak was born to Mehta Kalu and Mata Tripta, making it among the holiest Sikh shrines. A first gurdwara was raised in the sixteenth century by the Guru's grandson Baba Dharam Chand and the present structure was commissioned by Ranjit Singh in 1819–20; the site was the scene of the Nankana massacre of 20 February 1921, in which 86 Sikhs were killed, and is now managed by the Pakistan Sikh Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee.

name: Gurdwara Panja Sahib
deity: Guru Granth Sahib (handprint of Guru Nanak)
builtDisplay: 19th c. (Hari Singh Nalwa; Maharaja Ranjit Singh)
significance: A major Sikh shrine at Hasan Abdal built around a boulder bearing what tradition holds to be Guru Nanak's handprint, from his visit with Bhai Mardana in the summer of 1521. The general Hari Singh Nalwa is credited with the first gurdwara on the spot and Maharaja Ranjit Singh later rebuilt it in Mughal idiom; the sacred spring here was already recorded by the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang in the seventh century.
story: It is told that a local ascetic refused Guru Nanak water and hurled a rock at him, which the Guru stopped with his open palm, leaving his handprint in the stone and releasing a spring.

name: Mahaparinirvana Temple, Kushinagar
builtDisplay: present temple 1956, over ancient stupa remains
significance: Marks the place where the Buddha is held to have attained parinirvana, one of the four principal Buddhist pilgrimage sites. Ashoka is said to have visited around 260 BCE and raised stupas here; the vaulted chamber sheltering the 6.1 m reclining Buddha was in place by the Gupta period, the ruins were excavated in 1877 and restored by the ASI, and the present temple was built by the Government of India in 1956.
story: Buddhist tradition relates that after forty-five years of teaching the Buddha reached Kushinagar gravely ill, ordained his last disciple, and passed into parinirvana lying on his right side with his head to the north.

name: Jetavana, Shravasti
builtDisplay: built in the Buddha's lifetime by Anathapindika
significance: The most famous vihara of early Buddhism, given by the merchant Anathapindika outside Savatthi, where the Buddha spent nineteen of his forty-five rains retreats and delivered the majority of his discourses. The complex held the Gandhakuti, gardens and a pond, and Tibetan accounts describe sixty large and sixty small halls; an inscription of 1128 CE records the Gahadavala king Govindachandra renewing grants to it, showing it was still active in the medieval period.
story: Prince Jeta joked that he would sell his park only if it were covered in gold coins, so Anathapindika had cartloads of gold laid over the ground until the prince relented and donated the gateway himself.

name: Sankissa
deity: Gautama Buddha (site of the descent from the heavens)
significance: One of the eight great Buddhist pilgrimage places, revered as the spot where the Buddha returned to earth after teaching the Abhidhamma to his mother in the Tushita heaven. Ashoka set up a pillar with an elephant capital, a stupa and a temple here in the third century BCE, and the ruins of Buddhist monasteries and later Hindu monuments were surveyed by Alexander Cunningham in 1842.
story: The texts say Indra built three ladders down from Mount Meru so that the Buddha and his retinue could descend to earth at Sankissa on the Mahapavarana festival day.

name: Kaushambi (Kosambi)
builtDisplay: fortified city, 8th c. BCE – 2nd c. CE
significance: Capital of the Vatsa mahajanapada on the Yamuna and a canonical Buddhist centre: the Buddha visited repeatedly and stayed at four monasteries here, including the Ghositarama, and a famous schism among the monks took place at the city. Occupied from roughly the twelfth century BCE to about 600 CE, its fortifications and palace were built in six phases, and Ashoka raised a pillar here whose edict is addressed to the officials of Kausambi.

name: Bharhut Stupa
builtDisplay: railings c. 125–100 BCE, gateway c. 100–75 BCE (Shunga period)
significance: A stupa celebrated for the finest surviving sculpture of the aniconic phase of Buddhist art, where the Buddha is indicated by the dharma wheel, the bodhi tree or an empty throne rather than shown in person. The mound may go back to Ashoka in the third century BCE, while the stone railing and torana gateway were added in the Shunga period, the gateway commissioned by King Dhanabhuti; Buddhism continued at the site until about the twelfth century CE.

name: Bavikonda
significance: A hilltop Buddhist monastery complex of stupas and viharas about 16 km from Visakhapatnam, protected as a monument and dated to the third century BCE. Excavations by the state archaeology department yielded pottery, coins, tiles, inscriptions and relic caskets, among them an urn holding a piece of bone taken to be a relic of the Buddha; the name means 'hill of wells' in Telugu, after its rainwater cisterns.

name: Thotlakonda
significance: A Nikaya Buddhist establishment on a hill 128 m above the sea that served as a teaching centre and a staging point for pilgrims travelling by sea, its worship centred on aniconic symbols such as the Buddha's footprints. Spotted during an Indian Navy aerial survey and excavated between 1988 and 1993, it produced Satavahana lead coins, Roman silver coins and twelve inscriptions, and appears to have been supported by traders and local lay Buddhists rather than royal patrons; the stupa, damaged by monsoon rains in 2019, was restored by 2021.

name: Salihundam
deity: Gautama Buddha (stupas; images of Tara and Marichi)
significance: A hillock in ancient Kalinga carrying four stupas and a large monastic complex, showing that Buddhism flourished here in the second and third centuries and that Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana practice all left traces, including sculptures of Tara and Marichi. Discovered by Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy in 1919 and later excavated by the state, the site is regarded as a point from which Buddhism spread towards Sumatra and the Far East; the village's older name Salipetaka means 'rice emporium'.

name: Guntupalli Caves
significance: A Buddhist complex near Kamavarapukota with rock-cut caves on two levels, an unusual brick chaitya hall built above ground around a stone stupa, and more than thirty smaller stupas on a terrace. The chaitya's carved stone entrance imitates wooden architecture in the manner of the Lomas Rishi cave; excavation recovered three relic caskets with gold, silver and crystal beads, a bronze Padmapani, and casket inscriptions dated to the ninth and tenth centuries CE.

name: Pandavleni Caves
deity: Gautama Buddha (viharas and chaitya; later bodhisattva and Tirthankara images)
builtDisplay: 1st c. BCE – 2nd c. CE (Kshatrapa and Satavahana)
significance: Twenty-four rock-cut caves above Nashik, mostly viharas with one chaitya, excavated over several centuries as donations by rulers, merchants and an Indo-Greek donor. Cave 10 records the patronage of Nahapana's viceroy Ushavadata around 120 CE and Cave 3, the largest vihara, was given by the Satavahana queen Gotami Balasiri in memory of her son Gautamiputra Satakarni around 150 CE; the inscriptions document the contest between the Satavahanas and the Western Satraps, and the site preserves an early rock-cut water system.

name: Aurangabad Caves
deity: Gautama Buddha (stupas, bodhisattvas and Vajrayana goddesses)
significance: Twelve rock-cut Buddhist shrines carved out of soft basalt nine kilometres from the city, arranged in western, eastern and northern groups. They combine early stupa worship with Mahayana sculpture and Vajrayana goddesses alongside figures such as Durga and Ganesha, and although overshadowed by Ajanta and Ellora, scholars read them as a link between those two sites; they are protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.

name: Pitalkhora Caves
significance: Fourteen basalt cave monuments in two groups, four chaityas and ten viharas, counted among the earliest rock-cut architecture in India and lying about forty kilometres from Ellora. Inscriptions here range from roughly 250 BCE to the third and fourth centuries CE and later Mahayana paintings survive; the carved elephants, soldier figures and a damaged Gaja Lakshmi, together with an ancient rainwater harvesting system, helped establish the chronology of the wider Ajanta–Ellora region.

name: Bedse Caves
significance: A small basalt cave group of the Satavahana period whose chaitya (Cave 7) encloses a comparatively large stupa and whose vihara (Cave 11) has an unusual apsidal plan with nine cells. The carving is rich in gavaksha motifs and columns with animal capitals, and an inscription records the gift of Pushyanka, son of Ananda Sethi of Nashik; regular whitewashing and painting ordered for British visitors until about 1861 destroyed the original plaster and murals.

name: Bagh Caves
significance: Nine rock-cut monasteries cut into perpendicular sandstone in Dhar district, of which five survive, laid out on quadrangular plans comparable to Ajanta. A copperplate found in Cave 2 records repairs by Maharaja Subandhu in Gupta year 167 (487 CE); the ASI worked on the monuments for seventeen years, and the tempera paintings were lifted in 1982 and moved to the Gujari Mahal Archaeological Museum at Gwalior.

name: Mindrolling Monastery
significance: The Indian seat of the Nyingma monastery of Mindrolling, re-established near Clement Town in Dehradun in 1965 by Khochhen Rinpoche and a small group of monks after the loss of the original monastery in Tibet. It houses the Ngagyur Nyingma College, one of the largest Buddhist institutes in India, and a 190-foot stupa dedicated to world peace that Khochhen Rinpoche inaugurated in 2002.

name: Shri Mahavirji
significance: The foremost Digambara Jain pilgrimage centre of Rajasthan, built in the seventeenth century by the merchant Amar Chand Bilala around an image of Mahavira said to be more than a thousand years old. Other Tirthankara images are also enshrined, and the temple draws millions of pilgrims a year.
story: A Meena dairy farmer named Krapa Ram is said to have found his cow spilling her milk over a mound near Chandanpur; when the villagers dug there they uncovered the image of Mahavira around which the temple grew.

name: Padampura Jain Temple
significance: A Digambara Jain atishaya kshetra at Shivdaspura, some 35 km from Jaipur, built in white marble with an 85-foot spire around a red stone image of the sixth Tirthankara Padmaprabha. The image was unearthed in 1944 by a farmer, Moola Jat, while digging the foundation of his house, and the temple was raised the following year with land and funds given by the businessman Mahorilal Godha.
story: Villagers hold that once the image was found the settlement's water scarcity ended, its cattle stopped dying and its harvests grew abundant, and that prayer here relieves physical and mental affliction.

name: Kulpakji
significance: An ancient Shvetambara Jain temple at Kolanupaka whose foundation is placed in the ninth century, when the Kalachuri ruler Shankaragana granted it twelve villages, and which flourished further under the Rashtrakutas. Its interior is finished in red sandstone and white marble; more than twenty inscriptions link it to the Kanur Gana monastic lineage, and a Kannada inscription of 1125 CE from the Western Chalukya emperor Someshvara III records its standing.
story: Shvetambara tradition credits the original temple to the legendary emperor Bharata Chakravartin.

name: Muktagiri
builtDisplay: temples 13th–14th c.; site from the 10th c.
significance: A Digambara Jain pilgrimage site of fifty-two temples on the Madhya Pradesh–Maharashtra border, established in the tenth century. Its oldest structure is a cave temple of the thirteenth or fourteenth century with an arched, lotus-carved entrance and some fifty-six Tirthankara images, while the seven-hooded Parshvanatha of the twenty-sixth temple is regarded as its finest sculpture.
story: It is said that saffron and sandalwood rain down here once every eighth century, and that whoever visits, of whatever faith, attains nirvana.

name: Manakamana Temple
significance: A two-storeyed pagoda shrine of the goddess Bhagawati in Gorkha district, founded in 1678 by Arman Rayamajhi during the Gorkha kings' rule and served by priests who must descend from Lakhan Thapa Magar. It has survived the earthquakes of 1934, 1988 and 2015, and was extensively rebuilt between 2015 and 2018 with fourteen kilograms of gold used in the restoration.
story: Tradition says a Gorkha queen's hidden divine power was known only to the priest Lakhan Thapa; after the king died and she committed sati, a farmer's plough split a stone that ran with blood and milk, and Lakhan Thapa performed rites there and raised the shrine.

name: Dakshinkali Temple
significance: A temple of Kali in her Dakshina aspect in the southern part of the Kathmandu valley, one of the valley's most visited goddess shrines. The name plays on dakshina, the offering given with the right hand, matching an iconography in which two of the goddess's right hands make gestures of blessing and boon-giving.
story: It is told that Yama, the lord of death, was seized with terror at the mere sound of Kali's name, so that those who worship her here are said to overcome death itself.

name: Doleshwor Mahadeva Temple
significance: A pagoda-roofed Shiva shrine in Suryabinayak Municipality of Bhaktapur district, drawing large gatherings at Shivaratri, Teej and Balachaturdasi. The temple's early history is not documented, though it is popularly linked to the Mahabharata.

name: Halesi Mahadev
builtDisplay: natural cave shrine, attested from the 12th c.
significance: A natural cave sanctuary in Khotang, sacred at once to Hindus as a seat of Mahadev, to Buddhists as the Maratika cave, and to the Kirat peoples, and often called 'the Pashupatinath of the east'. It appears in Himalayan literature from the twelfth century onwards; Buddhist accounts hold that Mandarava and Padmasambhava recovered terma concealed here by the dakini Sangwa Yeshe and attained the accomplishment of long life.
story: Hindu tradition says Shiva took refuge in this cave while fleeing the demon Bhasmasur, one account holding that he remained hidden there for six thousand years.

name: Baraha Chhetra
significance: One of Nepal's oldest shrines, named in the Puranas and the Mahabharata, standing at the Koshi confluence and dedicated to Vishnu in his boar incarnation. Statues found here are over 1,500 years old; the domed temple standing today was rebuilt by Juddha Shamsher Jang Bahadur Rana after the 1934 earthquake, within a complex of nine temples including shrines to Lakshmi, Panchayan, Guruvarah, Suryavarah, Kokawarah and Nageshwar.
story: The Varaha story tells that Vishnu, taking the form of a boar, lifted the earth out of the netherworld on his tusk and afterwards rested with Lakshmi at this Himalayan river confluence.

name: Maya Devi Temple, Lumbini
builtDisplay: Ashokan brick temple c. 249 BCE; timber shrine of the 6th c. BCE beneath
significance: Marks the birthplace of Gautama Buddha and ranks with Bodh Gaya, Sarnath and Kushinagar among the four holiest Buddhist places, set beside its sacred pushkarani pool and garden. Ashoka built a brick temple here around 249 BCE, and excavations from 2010 by UNESCO, Durham University and Nepal's Department of Archaeology uncovered a timber shrine of the sixth century BCE beneath it, showing successive rebuildings from the Buddha's own lifetime; the temple houses the marker stone and a nativity relief.
story: Tradition holds that Queen Maya, travelling to her father's kingdom, gave birth to the Buddha under a sal tree at Lumbini and died seven days later, to be reborn in the Tushita heaven.

name: Nyatapola Temple
significance: The tallest temple in Nepal, a five-tiered pagoda on Bhaktapur's Taumadhi Square dedicated to the tantric goddess Siddhi Lakshmi. King Bhupatindra Malla commissioned it and the whole structure was raised in about six months between December 1701 and July 1702, with workers and materials drawn from across his kingdom.
story: The goddess Bhagavati, in her form as Siddhi Lakshmi, is said to have overpowered the destructive Bhairava and carried him in her hand; the king built the temple facing Bhairava's shrine, its stone guardians ranged in pairs on each terrace, each pair held to be ten times stronger than the one below.

name: Krishna Mandir, Patan
significance: A seventeenth-century stone shikhara temple raised by King Siddhi Narsingh Malla in Patan Durbar Square, unusual in a valley of pagoda-roofed shrines. Badly damaged in the April 2015 earthquake, it was restored and reopened to worshippers in 2018.

name: Taleju Temple, Kathmandu
significance: The royal sanctuary of Taleju Bhawani, tutelary goddess of the Malla kings, built by Mahendra Malla in 1564 within Hanuman Dhoka at Kathmandu Durbar Square. It opens to lay devotees only once a year during Dashain, and among its treasures was a seventeenth-century ceremonial necklace now in the Art Institute of Chicago.

name: Punakha Dzong
deity: Drukpa Kagyu (relics of the southern Drukpa lineage)
significance: The second oldest and second largest dzong in Bhutan, built in 1637–38 by Ngawang Namgyal, the first Zhabdrung Rinpoche, with Zowe Palep as architect. It keeps the sacred relics of the southern Drukpa lineage, served as the seat of government until the capital moved to Thimphu in 1955, and has hosted every royal coronation since 1907.
story: It is told that the Zhabdrung had the architect sleep beneath a small structure housing a Buddha image, and in a dream he saw a palace for Guru Rinpoche so clearly that he built the dzong from memory, without ever drawing a plan.

name: Tashichho Dzong
deity: Drukpa Kagyu monastery and seat of government
significance: The fortress-monastery on the Wang Chhu that houses Bhutan's throne room and government offices and serves as the traditional summer seat of the central monastic body. The first Do-Ngön Dzong was built on a different site in 1216 by Lama Gyalwa Lhanapa; Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal took it over in 1641 and renamed it, a new dzong was raised at the present site after a fire in 1772, and the third king, Jigme Dorji Wangchuck, rebuilt it from 1962 after the capital moved from Punakha, with consecration in 1968.

name: Chimi Lhakhang
significance: A small temple on a round hillock near Lobesa, founded in 1499 by Ngawang Chogyal, fourteenth abbot of Ralung, on a site blessed by his cousin Drukpa Kunley. It is Bhutan's best known fertility shrine: women come for blessings to conceive and for names for unborn children, and pilgrims are touched on the head with a wooden phallus that Kunley is said to have brought from Tibet.
story: Tradition holds that Drukpa Kunley subdued a demoness here with his magic thunderbolt of wisdom and sealed her in a rock, and that he and his dog Sachi passed into heaven, their reclining images now enshrined in the prayer hall.

name: Jambay Lhakhang
significance: One of Bhutan's oldest temples, dedicated to Maitreya and ascribed to the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo in 659 CE, in the same group as the Jokhang at Lhasa and Kyichu in Paro. Padmasambhava is said to have visited it and King Sindhu Raja to have restored it; repaired and rebuilt many times since, it remains an active pilgrimage temple and hosts the Jambay Lhakhang Drup festival each October.
story: The legend says Songtsen Gampo raised 108 temples in a single day across Tibet, Bhutan and the borderlands to pin down a supine ogress whose limbs were blocking the spread of Buddhism, this temple standing on one of those points.
